extracted.intended_audience: British legislators, statesmen, and the politically engaged public concerned with the French Revolution (late 18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A political-philosophical critique of the French revolutionary constitution focusing on the executive, judicial, and military arrangements and their practical consequences for liberty, order, and government. The page offers normative standards for how those institutions ought to be constituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive must have deliberative discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: “their first executive officer is to be a machine, without any sort of deliberative discretion in any one act of his function.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that making the executive a mere channel to the Assembly renders the office impotent and perilous; such an executor cannot properly direct measures and the office of intelligence becomes 'as nothing.' Anti-pattern: an executive reduced to an authorized reporter with no independent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive should be the fountain of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “The king of France is not the fountain of justice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how judges are not of the king's nomination and the king only authenticates choices; warns that depriving the sovereign of judicial authority reduces the office to a degrading administrative role (notary, jailer, hangman). Implies a criterion that executive authority should include genuine judicial prerogatives or complementary institutions to preserve dignity and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive must have means to reward service
rubrics_metrics.description: “What sort of person is a king to command executory service, who has no means whatsoever to reward it:—not in a permanent office; not in a grant of land; no, not in a pension of fifty pounds a year; not in the vainest and most trivial title?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that without the ability to confer honors, offices, or rewards, those who serve the executive will be motivated only by fear, undermining loyalty and zeal. Criterion: retain instruments of patronage/honor to secure effective executive service; anti-pattern: an executive with no reward power leading to fear-based obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive magistracy should inspire love and veneration
rubrics_metrics.description: “Executive magistracy ought to be constituted in such a manner that those who compose it should be disposed to love and to venerate those whom they are bound to obey.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that neglect or mere perverse obedience destroys wise counsel; selection and constitution of executive offices should cultivate loyalty and respect, not hatred or contempt. Examples invoked: historical ministers who served despite personal dislike of monarchs (Richelieu, Mazarin, Pitt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should be chosen by affairs not affections; act in trust for sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: “These ministers, who were chosen by affairs, not by affections, acted in the name of and in trust for kings, and not as their avowed constitutional and ostensible masters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: ministers ought to be appointed for competence and national interest, acting as trustees of the sovereign (or constitution), not as independent constitutional masters. Anti-pattern: ministers who owe position to revolutionary creators and therefore serve other masters or factional interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive should possess some control over peace and war
rubrics_metrics.description: “For instance, among many others, it was in your power to leave to your king the right of peace and war.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While acknowledging danger, argues that retaining the prerogative of peace and war with the executive (or providing indirect correctives and controls) helps prevent foreign intrigue and personal negotiation between foreign potentates and legislators. Criterion: reserve clear foreign-affairs competence to prevent factional foreign influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid maintaining both a real and a fictitious government
rubrics_metrics.description: “You have settled, by an economy as perverted as the policy, two establishments of government,—one real, one fictitious: both maintained at a vast expense; but the fictitious at, I think, the greatest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: institutional designs should avoid creating parallel 'fictitious' authorities (ceremonial offices without real power) that are costly and useless. Guidance: if ceremonial forms persist, make them useful instruments to ends rather than mere pageantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicature must be independent, permanent, and a check on power
rubrics_metrics.description: “They possessed one fundamental excellence: they were independent. ... They held for life. Indeed, they may be said to have held by inheritance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues the old parliaments' independence and permanence provided certainty, stability, protection of law and private property, and a corrective to arbitrary power. Criterion: judges should have tenure and institutional independence to resist capricious legislative or executive interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid elective, temporary, local judges for important tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: “elective, temporary, local judges, such as you have contrived, exercising their dependent functions in a narrow society, must be the worst of all tribunals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains this design invites partisanship, faction, and partiality against strangers, the rich, and minorities; ballots and short tenures produce suspicion rather than impartiality. Criterion: prefer stable, less-localized judicial appointment structures for fair justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain power to remonstrate in judicial or neutral institutions, not the executor
rubrics_metrics.description: “You ought never to suffer remonstrance from him who is to execute.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vesting remonstrance (a check on decrees) in the executor is judged absurd—either remove the power or give the executor more authority. Criterion: checks on legislature should be lodged in institutions that are not subordinated to execution, to preserve separation of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not swear judges to obey ad hoc orders that override law
rubrics_metrics.description: “they are to be sworn to obey all the rules, orders, and instructions which from time to time they are to receive from the National Assembly. These if they submit to, they leave no ground of law to the subject.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that binding judges to obey changing instructions destroys the rule of law—legislation could be changed mid-case and local appointing authorities would be contradicted. Criterion: judicial oath and duty must not permit arbitrary alteration of legal rules by a separate appointing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative bodies and officers must be subject to law and coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those who execute public pecuniary trusts ought of all men to be the most strictly held to their duty...the administrative bodies are carefully exempted from the jurisdiction of these new tribunals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that exempting administrators from judicial jurisdiction places them above law and makes them instruments of oligarchy. Criterion: administrative authorities that manage public funds should be amenable to legal coercion and accountability; anti-pattern: placing administrative bodies 'above the law' to shield revolutionary leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: High court of state justice must be independent and not self-serving
rubrics_metrics.description: “If great care is not taken to form it in a spirit very different from that which has guided them in their proceedings relative to state offences, this tribunal...will extinguish the last sparks of liberty...If they wish to give to this tribunal any appearance of liberty and justice, they must not evoke from or send to it the causes relative to their own members, at their pleasure. They must also remove the seat of that tribunal out of the republic of Paris.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: a supreme/state court must not be subservient to the legislative inquirers, must not try matters involving the legislature's own members on demand, and should be geographically and institutionally removed from local factional pressures (e.g., away from Paris) to have credibility and avoid becoming an instrument of inquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army must be an instrument obedient to civilian command, not a deliberative body
rubrics_metrics.description: “The nature of things requires that the army should never act but as an instrument. The moment that, erecting itself into a deliberate body, it shall act according to its own resolutions, the government...will immediately degenerate into a military democracy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: preserve strict discipline and subordination of the military to civil authority; avoid conditions (committees, soldier assemblies) that convert the army into an independent political actor. Warns that military democracy historically devours its creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent irregular soldier committees, mutinous assemblies, and municipal usurpation of military authority
rubrics_metrics.description: “irregular consultations and turbulent committees formed in some regiments by the common soldiers and non-commissioned officers...the municipalities arrogate to themselves an authority over the troops...to break the officers...to give orders to the soldiers...to enslave the troops to the caprice of each of the cities”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: prohibit and remedy soldier-led committees, municipal interference in military command, and practices that humiliate or dispossess officers of authority. Anti-patterns include municipal trials of officers, driving officers from posts, and municipalities superseding military orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on renewed oaths or proclamations alone to restore military discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: “After the secretary at war had stated that the regiments had paid no regard to oaths...they propose—what? More oaths. They renew decrees and proclamations as they experience their insufficiency, and they multiply oaths in proportion as they weaken in the minds of men the sanctions of religion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: merely issuing more oaths and proclamations without enforcement mechanisms (courts, martial measures) is ineffective and may further erode moral sanctions; practical remedies should include enforcement and restoration of command authority rather than rhetorical reiteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should be consistent and not issued as occasional decrees (psephismata)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The vice of the ancient democracies, and one cause of their ruin, was, that they ruled, as you do, by occasional decrees, psephismata. This practice soon broke in upon the tenor and consistency of the laws; it abated the respect of the people towards them, and totally destroyed them in the end.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: legislate in ways that preserve continuity, consistency, and general jurisprudential principles rather than frequent ad hoc decrees. Short laws may be desirable, but overly brief or episodic legislation that leaves too much to discretion undermines legal stability.
